lead: An irreversible powered control has no natural feel: the actuator swallows the whole hinge moment and the stick is disconnected from the airloads. Q-feel puts feel back artificially, so stick force grows with dynamic pressure q = ½ρV² — light at low speed, firm at high speed. Tabs do the same aerodynamically: a small tab with a small hinge moment drives or lightens a large surface. Nearly every large transport has artificial feel of some kind, and tabs remain common on manual and boosted surfaces. Some syllabi treat this topic only briefly, inside powered controls.
prereq: You need: the chapter on powered flight controls for the irreversible powered system that has lost its natural feel.

sections.h3: Why feel must follow dynamic pressure

blocks.text: In an irreversible powered control the actuator carries the whole hinge moment. Airloads no longer push back on the stick, so feel must be made on purpose. A plain spring is the obvious answer and the wrong one: the response changes with speed, the spring does not.

blocks.where: q is dynamic pressure in Pa (N/m²); ρ is air density in kg/m³, about 1.225 at sea level in the standard atmosphere; V is true airspeed in m/s.

blocks.text: Hinge moment grows roughly with q times deflection. At 250 m/s, q is about eleven times its value at 75 m/s. A fixed spring would make the aircraft razor-sharp at high speed and sluggish at low speed. Q-feel makes the spring rate a function of q, so the stick force for a given stick movement follows the square of airspeed, as natural feel would on a manual aircraft.

sections.h3: The Q-feel chain: pitot to stick

items: Sensing: pitot minus static gives impact pressure, read by a capsule or the air data computer.
Feel computer: scales q into a gradient, e.g. 3 N per kilopascal.
Bellows: q moves a spring cartridge anchor in the stick circuit, stiffening it as q rises.
Spring gradient: stick travel x gives force F = k(q)·x.
Bob weight: a mass on the linkage adds force with load factor n — feel per g that no speed sensor gives.
Trim release: unloads the feel unit so the pilot can shift the neutral point; on release the present position is zero force.

blocks.text: The unit is called artificial or synthetic feel. It only loads the stick, never the surface.

sections.h3: Servo tabs and the tab family

blocks.text: A tab is a small aerofoil hinged at the trailing edge of a main surface. Its chord is short, so its own hinge moment is small, but its lift acts on a long arm behind the surface hinge. A tab can therefore move something much bigger than itself.

In a servo tab system the pilot's linkage drives only the tab; the main surface is free to float on its hinge. The pilot moves the tab, say trailing edge up; the airflow pushes the tab down, and that force on a long arm behind the surface hinge swings the main surface trailing edge down, the opposite way to the tab. A small stick force moves a large surface, so a large manual aircraft can be flown by tab. The servo tab is a driving device.

head: Tab
Moves
Job
rows: opposite to the surface, only when the spring load is exceeded

blocks.text: The anti-servo tab is the mirror image: geared to move with the surface, it increases hinge moment and resists the pilot. That resistance is feel, and it damps the surface against gusts. An all-moving tailplane (stabilator) pivots near its own aerodynamic centre, so its hinge moment is small and the stick would feel too light; light aircraft with a stabilator, such as the Piper PA-28 Cherokee, carry an anti-servo tab for that reason. Memory line: a servo tab saves muscle, an anti-servo tab gives back information.

figure.caption: Left: the Q-feel force of the worked example, counted from zero at the 75 m/s trim: 31.0 N at 150 m/s and 104.5 N at 250 m/s, because force follows dynamic pressure. Right: a servo tab deflects opposite to its surface and drives it; an anti-servo tab moves with the surface and adds feel.

examples.question: A Q-feel system gives 3 N of stick force per kilopascal of dynamic pressure above the trim value. The aircraft is trimmed (zero stick force) at 75 m/s. Find the stick force needed to hold the same stick displacement at 150 m/s and at 250 m/s, in air of density 1.225 kg/m³.
steps: At 75 m/s: q₁ = ½ × 1.225 × 75² = 3445 Pa = 3.445 kPa. This is the trim point, where the stick force is zero.
Check: q rose 4 times from 75 to 150 m/s because q carries V²; the force does not rise 4 times because it is counted from the trim value.
examples.answer: The pilot needs 31.0 N at 150 m/s and 104.5 N at 250 m/s, both measured from zero force at the 75 m/s trim.
examples.check:
rho = 1.225
k = 3.0
def q(v):
    return 0.5 * rho * v * v
q1 = q(75); q2 = q(150)
print(round(q1/1000, 3))
print(round(q2/1000, 3))
print(round(k*(q2-q1)/1000, 2))

traps: Swapping servo and anti-servo: the servo tab moves opposite to the surface and drives it; the anti-servo tab moves with the surface and adds feel.
Matching airspeed to density wrongly: use local density with true airspeed, or sea-level density with equivalent airspeed.
Leaving q in pascals when the gradient is per kilopascal — divide by 1000 first.
Thinking Q-feel changes the aircraft's response. It changes only pilot force; the surface still deflects as commanded.
Confusing the q-bellows (feel per unit speed) with the bob weight (feel per g).

quiz.q: Define dynamic pressure with its formula and SI unit.
quiz.a: q = ½ρV², in pascals (N/m²); ρ in kg/m³, V in m/s.

quiz.q: Which tab drives a surface, and which adds feel?
quiz.a: Servo tab drives; anti-servo tab adds feel.

quiz.q: Why does a plain spring make a fast aircraft over-sensitive?
quiz.a: High q gives much more lift per degree of surface, so a constant spring force commands a big manoeuvre for little effort.

quiz.q: A Q-feel unit gives 2.5 N per kPa of dynamic pressure, counted from zero. Find the stick force at 200 m/s, ρ = 1.225 kg/m³.
Airspeed rises from 90 m/s to 135 m/s. By what factor does a Q-feel force counted from zero q change?
In a pull-up at constant speed, n rises from 1 to 3 but q is fixed. Why add a bob weight?
quiz.a: Q-feel reads airspeed only, not g. The bob weight adds force with normal acceleration, so the pilot feels the manoeuvre.

beyond: Not for the exam. Fly-by-wire aircraft build the same gradient in software: the control law computes feel from q, load factor, Mach and flap position, and a motor loads the sidestick. Simulators use electric control loading. Search artificial feel system and control loading system.
